title: Reconfiguring Procedural Knowledge for Compositional Robot Skill Adaptation
claim: Retrieval ignores connectivity and structured representations need retraining; ours composes view-consistent transitions from sparse specifications into executable sequences.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right: inputs, prior approaches stacked, ours with materialization
description: Three vertical panels on light grey backgrounds. The left panel, 'Sparse Governing Information', shows a task specification as a three-step kitchen scene (microwave, kettle, cabinet) with arrows. Below it is a procedure specification with stacked skill records (closed to opened) and view thumbnails from simulation. The middle panel stacks two prior approaches. 'Behavior Retrieval' shows a red 'fail' and a dashed 'missing bridge' warning between disconnected nodes. 'Structured procedural representations' shows graph chains with a yellow 'update required' warning and a deprecated versus updated task specification. The right panel, 'Reconfigurable Skill Policy (Ours)', shows a task specification splitting via arrows into three coloured view-level change graphs (brown, red, blue). These merge into a 'Materialize' graph and lead to a Franka robot rendering in the environment. Red and yellow warnings draw the eye in the middle panel.
caption: Conceptual overview of reconfigurable skill policy under sparse governing information. (left) Sparse task evidence specifies desired changes, while procedure-side evidence provides task-agnostic skill records observed through multiple procedure views. (middle) Behavior retrieval accesses stored records independently, whereas structured procedural approaches expose connectivity among reusable behaviors. (right) \ours{} converts observed view-level changes into a compositional query and materializes a task-specific executable skill sequence over view-consistent procedural transitions.
abstract: General-purpose behavior models increasingly internalize broad procedural knowledge during training, making their adaptation to new goals and skill interfaces less a problem of learning entirely new behaviors than of reconfiguring existing competence. We study this capability as reconfigurability, the ability to realize new behaviors by cost-efficiently restructuring existing components and relations under sparse governing information, where task specifications provide high-level goals and procedure specifications expose a limited set of reusable factors, leaving the concrete bindings and compositions required for execution underdetermined. We propose RecPo, a framework that represents skills task-agnostically through multiple procedure views and materializes executable skill sequences by composing stored transitions to realize task-specific changes. RecPo maintains a procedure knowledge base of skill-induced transitions, with each view exposing a reusable factor and preserving local skill connectivity. At deployment, it interprets task specifications through the same views and resolves the resulting compositional queries over the stored relations to bind skills for execution. On long-horizon tasks in an extended Franka Kitchen benchmark, RecPo achieves 91.9% ordered completion with 1.0 ms of task inference per episode across varying procedure support and task-record sparsity. Real-robot studies further demonstrate adaptation through local memory edits without task-specific retraining.
